SBI2 / CytoData hackathon · Altair OPS0077 and Element A549

Cell Cycle Heterogeneity Findings

Can we read the cell cycle from morphology, and does removing it make perturbed cell populations less heterogeneous? This page collects the results in the order of the argument. Each section gives the answer first, then the evidence, then the notebook to open.

1What each part of the 4i clock contains

Answer. The clock (cc_phase, 0 = start of G1) runs G1, then S, then G2/M, and wraps back to G1. Measured DNA puts the 4N (G2/M) cells at 0.5 to 0.75, and the last quarter (0.75 to 1) is almost entirely 2N cells after division. Labelling the quarters "Early G1 / Late G1 / S / G2/M" therefore shifts every label by about one quarter.

correctionThis explains the G1 puzzle in item 6: a G1 accumulation adds cells to the 0.75 to 1 quarter, which the figure labels as "G2/M". CDK7 is an example: its "+10.8% G2/M" is a gain of 2N cells.

2How well each modality reads the cell cycle

Answer. Label-free phase contrast reads the cycle as well as the 4i antibody panel: both predict the clock to about 30 degrees, and phase contrast separates measured DNA state slightly better. In Element, imaging without the DNA stain reads the RNA clock about as well as the RNA clock itself separates DNA state.

A better phase-contrast model

Brian's gradient-boosted trees on the raw phase features predict the clock to 21.8 degrees (held out by tile), against 29.3 for our ridge on PCA-100. Most of the gain needs the raw features: on PCA-100 the same trees reach only 28.3, and a single-target neural network 26.8. How missing values are handled does not matter (21.7 vs 21.8). Predicting the DNA x pRb stages directly reaches balanced accuracy 0.59 (chance 0.25), but S phase stays hard (recall 0.24).

3Aligning the cell-cycle scores across regimes

Answer. Within OPS0077 the DNA-based 4i clocks are one clock. The markers-only clock runs the same way but is rotated by 142 degrees, and its stored origin is arbitrary. Across datasets only the S to G2/M arc aligns (OPS0077 to the Element RNA clock: +240 degrees, from DNA). The G1 arc cannot be aligned with the shared features we have, so we compare datasets through DNA-content classes and not through angles.

notebook 17

4Which knockouts shift the cell cycle

Answer. 81 of the 1,000 OPS0077 knockouts change the predicted cell-cycle distribution. DNA replication and mitosis genes gain 4N cells (CDC45 +10.5 points, MTBP +14.3, KIF23 +11.8). Ribosome, translation and chaperonin genes lose them (POLR1B -8.5, RPL and RPS genes, CCT complex), as expected for an arrest before S. The predicted change in 4N cells agrees with measured pRb on the same cells (rho 0.37).

Comparing fairly with NTC

  • Knockout cells are never in training, so NTC must be scored out of fold too, and all NTC cells must be used (a third of them have no measured clock but the knockout cells were never filtered that way).
  • The null is NTC guides pooled to the knockout's cell count. With this reference CDK7 and CCNB1 shift by about +3 to +4 points (not significant), not +7 to +11.
  • For CCNB1 the 4N gain is real: measured DAPI gives +4.3 points.

Checked against measured DNA

For 111 knockouts (81 predicted shifters and 30 calibration knockouts) we measured DNA from DAPI. The predicted change in 4N cells matches the measured change: Spearman 0.76, slope 1.01. 42 of the 81 predicted shifts are confirmed at FDR 5%, 41 of them in the predicted direction. Most are losses of 4N cells (ribosome biogenesis, proteasome, chaperone and splicing genes such as HSPA9, IMP4, PSMD4, SRSF3); the confirmed gains are replication genes (MTBP +17.0, MCM7 +12.2, CDC45 +8.4, POLA2 +7.9 points). 7 of the 30 calibration knockouts also shift, always in the predicted direction, so the library misses some real shifts (the largest is the mitotic kinesin KIF11, +19.5 points).

Adding the other 47 arrest-list genes (158 knockouts, not selected on a predicted shift) keeps the agreement (Spearman 0.64 for the 47 alone, 0.78 over all 158). Measured, the arrest list behaves as follows: the S group gains 4N cells (median +4.7 points), the G1 group gains 2N cells (+6.1, mostly not significant one by one), and the G2/M group loses 4N cells (-2.5), the opposite of a G2/M arrest. Only CDC45 gains. These knockouts are not hidden as binucleate cells either (10.0% vs 10.4% in NTC; only KIF23 is clearly higher, 31%). So phase contrast was right not to see a G2/M arrest for them.

With the better model

Rerunning the library with gradient boosting finds 194 knockouts with a changed cycle distribution (73 of the 81 ridge hits among them). Agreement with measured pRb is unchanged (rho 0.38), and so is the heterogeneity result (spread -2.75%, separation from NTC unchanged). Most hits gain cells in "G1 after division" and lose G2 cells; the largest group of new hits is ribosome, translation and splicing genes. The extra hits are a more sensitive call under the same null, and a few of them (olfactory, taste-receptor and keratin-associated genes) are probably not expressed in A549.

Against measured DNA the gradient-boosting predictions are also better: Spearman 0.84 vs 0.78 over the 158 measured knockouts, and better in the subsets not chosen from either model (arrest list 0.70 vs 0.64, calibration 0.71 vs 0.63). The 8 hits only ridge calls confirm 0 times. We then measured DNA for the other 111 hits only gradient boosting calls. Over all 269 measured knockouts, 33 of its 121 extra hits are confirmed (27%), against 41 of 73 (56%) for hits both runs call and 5 of 67 (7%) for knockouts neither calls, and the rank correlation is 0.80 vs 0.74. The extra hits are real but weaker shifts. A 4N classifier trained on NTC reads knockout cells as well as NTC cells (CCNB1, MCM3 and CENPC, 1,353 cells: AUC 0.963 vs 0.968), so the model does not break on perturbed cells.

The arrest list against its expected arrest phase

S-phase genes behave as expected: 8 of 9 gain 4N cells (p = 3e-5 vs the rest of the library). The G1 and G2/M groups do not differ from the library. Several genes look misassigned (RRM1, POLE and RPA2 are replication genes listed under G1; CCNB1 is the mitotic cyclin listed under G1; CDC45 is listed under G2/M).

Brian's item 6: are G1-arrested cells misclassified?

  • explainedThe main reason is the quarter labels (section 1): G1 cells after division sit at 0.75 to 1.
  • testedThe hypertrophy idea is not supported. Within NTC the largest 2N cells are over-called as 4N (15.6% vs 3.4% of all 2N cells). But measured-2N knockout cells, although larger than NTC 2N cells in 148 of 158 knockouts (about 17% more area), are not called 4N more often (median excess -1.0 point; no relation with size, rho 0.09; the 26 G1-list knockouts range from -3.4 to +3.2 points). Brian's DNA floor changes no knockout by more than 0.63 points, and size corrections lower agreement with measured DNA (0.86 to 0.74 and 0.67).

5Regressing the cell cycle out: does heterogeneity go down?

Answer. The cycle is a few percent of the variance in every modality. It concentrates in the top principal components, which is why those tighten by 10 to 30%, but over the whole space it is 3 to 7%. Removing it shrinks perturbed populations by about 1 to 5% and does not change how well they separate from controls.

Diego's item 7, extended

Diego found that regressing cc_phase out of NTC embeddings tightens the top PCs (4i: 28 / 26 / 33%; phase contrast: 9 / 19 / 9%). We reproduce this when features are z-scored and the cycle is fitted flexibly (4i: 25 / 31%, phase contrast: 11 / 14%; total over 50 PCs 7.4% and 4.4%). Two additions:

  • About half of the 4i effect comes from the score itself. cc_phase is built from the 4i markers and principal components of the pRb, Rb and p21 features. Removing measured DNA content alone, which is independent of both embeddings, gives 10% on the top 4i PCs instead of 19%. For phase contrast the score is independent of the features, and the effect is real but smaller.
  • Knockouts tighten like NTC on the top PCs. With up to 200 cells from each of the 1,000 knockouts and Brian's predicted clock, pooled knockout cells tighten by 16 / 22 / 6% on PC1 to PC3, against 20 / 22 / 6% for NTC with the same clock. On PC5, PC7 and PC9 they tighten less.
  • Removing the cycle barely moves knockouts toward NTC. Their distance from NTC in PC1 to PC10 (corrected for sampling noise) shrinks by a median of about 5%, nearly the same for cycle-shifting knockouts (6.9%) and the rest (4.9%). Replication knockouts keep most of their distance (MCM7 76%, POLA2 83%, POLE 84%). Knockout phenotypes in phase contrast are mostly not cell-cycle composition.
  • Which phase features carry the cycle. 168 of 1,726 features lose more than 10% of their variance; the strongest are nuclear and nucleolar phase intensity, lowest in late G1 and highest from late G2 into division. Size features are under-represented.

The three cycle-normalisation questions

  • Field and well heterogeneity: not reduced. With a measured clock, the between-well and between-field share of control morphology does not change (Element wells 1.67% before, 1.72% after). A reduction seen with a morphology-predicted cycle is circular.
  • Finding perturbations that change the cycle distribution: yes (81 knockouts in OPS0077; TNFa and CTNNB1 in Element with the measured RNA clock).
  • Telling them apart from perturbations that change the cells: yes. Splitting each morphology shift into a cycle-mix part and a matched-cycle part shows 790 knockouts change the cells, 80 change both, 1 changes only the cycle mix (HSPA14), 129 change neither.

6Element: the RNA clock mapped to morphology

Answer. Element imaging reads the RNA cell-cycle clock to a median of 37.5 degrees in held-out wells (95,868 control cells; a shuffled clock gives 77.9). The DNA stain carries most of it, the phospho-antibody panel adds some, and mitochondria, membrane, actin and shape do no better than the IgG negative controls. Imaging fails on one stretch, about 135 to 255 degrees, where cells have just divided: their DNA is back at 2N but their RNA still reads G2/M.

  • Largest cycle phenotypes. 319 of 990 features change by more than 0.5 SD reproducibly (none of the 194 IgG features). The biggest sit around division: phospho-p38 and phospho-ERK intensity rise (up to +1.4 SD), DNA-stain and pERK texture change, and nuclei shrink.
  • Perturbations. Morphology recovers the largest measured shift (CTNNB1 knockout: -3.5 and -5.1 points on the G2/M arc, predicted -2.3 and -5.0) but makes false calls (TGFBR2 knockout, TNFa). It ranks the size of shifts (rho 0.79 over 11 contrasts) but not reliably their direction.
  • Correlates in OPS0077. DNA-stain texture changes from 2N to S to 4N the same way in both datasets (94% same sign over 52 features). Granularity does not transfer. In OPS0077 the best phase-contrast markers of DNA state are intensity extremes of phase objects (effect size up to 1.64, not size-adjusted).
notebook 20

7The CROP-seq knockouts

Answer. The public CROP-seq data are knockout-level only. Scored with cell-cycle gene programmes learned on Element single cells, only 14 of 997 knockouts move a programme strongly (SMARCD1 most), the classic arrest genes are flat, and agreement with phase contrast is weak (rho about 0.1).
